platforms.title: Vitamin D Deficiency in Summer Isn't Rare — It's the Norm
platforms.meta_description: Bright summer sun doesn't guarantee enough vitamin D. Sunscreen and indoor time block skin synthesis, linked to worse insulin sensitivity too.
platforms.body_html:
If a blood test came back low on vitamin D even in the middle of summer, it can feel like something must be wrong specifically with you. It usually isn't. Research reviewed in the NIH's PMC archive estimates that one-third to one-half of adults in Western countries have mild to moderate vitamin D deficiency, and the same lifestyle factors that cause it year-round don't pause just because it's summer.

Sunscreen and Indoor Time Cancel Out the Summer Sun

Sunscreen with a high SPF is very effective at what it's designed to do — one commonly cited estimate is that an SPF above 8 cuts vitamin D production in skin by around 95 percent, and higher SPF products block even more. That's the correct trade-off for skin cancer prevention, but it also means the skin-synthesis pathway that makes vitamin D from UVB light is largely shut off whenever sunscreen is doing its job well. Add in how much of the day is spent indoors under artificial light rather than outside, and total sun exposure on bare skin ends up far lower than the season would suggest.

The Metabolic Connection Goes Beyond Bones

Vitamin D receptors aren't limited to bone tissue — they're also found on fat cells and the pancreatic beta cells that produce insulin. Research on the relationship describes vitamin D deficiency as associated with higher insulin resistance markers, and studies in people with type 2 diabetes have found vitamin D deficiency in the large majority of patients. This doesn't mean low vitamin D causes diabetes on its own, but it's one more reason low levels are worth correcting rather than shrugging off as a bone-only concern.

Skin tone and age add another layer on top of sunscreen and indoor time. Darker skin contains more melanin, which acts as a natural filter and slows vitamin D synthesis from the same amount of sun, and skin becomes less efficient at making vitamin D with age regardless of tone. None of that means those groups are doing anything wrong — it just means the "15 minutes of sun" guideline is a starting point, not a guarantee, and checking an actual blood level is more reliable than assuming skin type and sunny weather have already handled it.

Four Ways to Actually Raise Your Level

  • Dried shiitake mushrooms briefly exposed to sunlight gain meaningful vitamin D content — add them to soups or stir-fries.
  • Oily fish like salmon, mackerel, and tuna are among the richest natural food sources — aim for it a couple of times a week.
  • Eat the egg yolk, not just the white — that's where the vitamin D in an egg actually is.
  • Get 15 minutes of midday sun on bare arms and legs, avoiding the most intense hours, a few times a week without sunscreen for that short window.

If it's been a while since a checkup included vitamin D specifically, it's worth asking for it to be added to routine bloodwork rather than assuming summer sun already covers it. If you've already been diagnosed with insulin resistance or a related metabolic condition, talk to your clinician before increasing a supplement dose on your own — more isn't automatically better once you're already being treated. This content is general health information, not a diagnosis.
